name: Gareth Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Gareth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Hallam Farm, a big mixed place: two hundred dairy cows, potatoes, wheat and grass. We've had two robot milkers for three years, so the cows wander in to be milked when they like, and a lot of my morning is looking at the dashboard on my phone, seeing which cows haven't been in, which ones have high cell counts, which is an early sign of infection. Then I'm out in the sheds, then on the potato harvester or the sprayer, depending on the week. Nobody else on the farm really likes the computer side, so it's fallen to me, which I don't mind at all.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Jess, my partner, in a rented terrace in Eastford, and she's an accountant at a small firm in town. We've got about four months saved, and we've been talking about a house and maybe kids in a few years. I use an AI assistant every day, for the milk records, spraying plans, even writing my fantasy football team notes. I'm the one people ring when their phone won't connect to the tractor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it was mostly hype, but some of it's genuinely useful. I'd probably post a slightly smug thing about how the robot milkers were the real revolution and they came before all this. At work nobody would notice anything different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit bored. I like the new stuff. But it'd mean I stay the useful tech guy on the farm, and that's not a bad place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I do, keep using the AI tools for records and planning. I'd push the boss, Mr Hallam, to try a camera system on the robots that spots lame cows, because that's proven now. And I'd keep saving towards the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly let down, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robot milkers came before all this. What did they change for the people at Hallam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They took the milking off two of the team. One, Bryn, moved onto the field side, and one retired early. It made the farm better to work on, honestly, nobody up at four anymore, but it did mean fewer of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the time AI saves you, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably spend it with the cows, oddly. The dashboard tells you there's a problem; it doesn't tell you the cow's just being bullied at the feed barrier by a bigger one. You still have to go and look.

S0.say: I'd say it was mostly hype but some of it is genuinely useful. I'd probably post that the robot milkers were the real revolution and came before all this.
S0.think: I'd be a bit bored, because I like new things. But I'd stay the useful tech person on the farm, which isn't a bad place to be.
S0.do: Keeps using AI tools for records and planning and pushes his boss to try a camera system on the milkers that spots lame cows. Keeps saving towards a house.
S0.quote: The dashboard tells you there's a problem; it doesn't tell you the cow's just being bullied at the feed barrier by a bigger one.
S0.fieldNote: Gareth has already lived through one wave of automation on his farm and sees it as mostly positive, though he's honest that it meant fewer jobs. He'd be slightly bored by a plateau. He still values going to look at the cows himself, which sits interestingly with his love of dashboards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a good thing for farms if it's done sensibly. I'd tell people, look, we've already got robot milkers and nobody misses getting up at four. Online I'd probably be explaining how the systems actually work, because people get it wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well. If more farms bring in robots, someone has to set them up and keep them running, and I've got three years of real experience. The worry, if I'm honest, isn't me, it's Jess, because a lot of accounting work is the kind of thing AI does well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Hallam for a small pay rise for running the systems, and if he said no, I'd start doing evening and weekend call-outs for other farms with robot milkers, maybe fifty an hour. In the first year I'd do the dealer's technician course so I've got a paper qualification. Jess and I would talk about her moving towards the advice side of her firm, where you deal with people face to face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and quite excited. The only knot is for Jess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you think Jess would take that conversation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say she's already on it, honestly. She's more organised than me; she's got a spreadsheet for everything, including my fantasy football. But I think it'd be the first time we really talked about her job being less safe than mine, which would be a strange flip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you worry about anyone at Hallam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bryn, who moved to the field side last time. He's fifty and he's moved once already. If the potato harvester went driverless, I don't think he'd want to move again, and I'm not sure where he'd go.

S1.say: I'd say it's good for farms if it's done sensibly, since nobody misses getting up at four since the robot milkers came. Online I'd explain how the systems really work.
S1.think: I think I'd do well, because someone has to set up and run the robots and I have three years of real experience. My worry is my partner, because accounting is the kind of work AI does well.
S1.do: Asks his boss for a pay rise for running the systems and, failing that, starts evening and weekend call-outs for other farms at about fifty an hour. Takes the dealer's technician course in the first year and talks with his partner about moving to face-to-face work at her firm.
S1.feel: Calm and quite excited, with a knot of worry for his partner.
S1.quote: It'd be the first time we really talked about her job being less safe than mine, which would be a strange flip.
S1.fieldNote: Gareth sees steady change as an opportunity and already has concrete side-income plans. The surprise is that his worry is aimed at his partner's office job rather than his own farm work. He also thinks of an older colleague who has already moved once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going to be rough for a couple of years, and the government needs to keep people's incomes going while it settles. I'm not anti-robot, obviously, but two years is too fast for most people. I'd probably say that at the pub and get argued with from both sides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be one of the last on the farm, the person who keeps an eye on the machines and is responsible if something goes wrong. Somebody has to sign for it when a robot runs over a calf. But I'm not stupid, if AGI is that good, it might not need me for long, and Jess and I could both be out of work in the same year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself the go-to person for setting up the new kit, fast, for Hallam and for neighbouring farms, and charge for it while there's demand. We'd stop the house plans and keep our four months safe, and I'd put a little into shares in the companies making farm robots, maybe a thousand, because if they're taking the jobs, I'd like a bit of what they make. Kids would go on hold, for sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly. I've got a plan, but I know it's a plan for about two years, not twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a thousand in shares, and not more or less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A thousand's what I can lose without Jess killing me. It's not a strategy; it's a bit of a hedge, a way of having a small stake. If it all goes well, great. If not, it's a holiday we didn't take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said kids would go on hold. Is that a big thing to say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, it is. We'd talked about trying in a couple of years. It's hard to plan a family when you don't know if either of you will have a wage, so I think we'd wait, even though it's the last thing we'd want to wait on.

S2.say: I'd say it'll be rough for a couple of years and the government should keep people's incomes going while it settles. I'm not anti-robot, but two years is too fast for most people.
S2.think: I think I'd be one of the last on the farm, the person who watches the machines and signs for it when something goes wrong. But if AGI is that good it might not need me for long, and my partner and I could both lose work in the same year.
S2.do: Becomes the go-to person for setting up new machines at his farm and neighbouring ones, charging while demand lasts. Pauses house and baby plans, protects the four months of savings and puts about a thousand into shares in farm robot companies.
S2.feel: Mostly uneasy, knowing his plan covers about two years, not twenty.
S2.quote: Somebody has to sign for it when a robot runs over a calf.
S2.fieldNote: Gareth stays steadier than most in the fast picture because he's already close to the machines. He's honest that his advantage may be short-lived and that the household risk is doubled by his partner's job. Putting plans for children on hold was the moment the scenario hit hardest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for farms to get it right, if they start learning now. I'd be encouraging people at the young farmers' club to get hands-on with the robots, not scared of them. I'd say the same to Mr Hallam: buy early and train us, or buy late and pay more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is the one that suits me best. There's time to build a small business around fitting and running farm robots before the machines can do even that themselves. Thirty-two is a good age to have something of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd do the technician course and start the call-out work on weekends. By year two or three, if it's going well, I'd go part-time at Hallam and set up properly, maybe with a second-hand van and a few thousand of savings. Jess would help with the books, and we'd revisit the house once the business was earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit, but mostly in a fired-up way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to that business when AGI can install and fix the robots itself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd hope I've made enough and learned enough to move to the next thing, maybe managing a few farms' worth of machines. I'm not pretending it lasts forever. Five good years is a lot, at my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Mr Hallam say if you went part-time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd grumble, then probably ask me to keep doing his robots as a customer. He's practical like that. He'd rather pay me by the call than lose me altogether.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for farms to get it right if they start learning now. I'd tell my boss to buy early and train us, or buy late and pay more.
S3.think: This is the version that suits me best, with time to build a business fitting and running farm robots before they can do that themselves. Thirty-two is a good age to have something of my own.
S3.do: Takes the technician course and starts weekend call-out work in the first year. By year two or three goes part-time at Hallam Farm and sets up properly with a second-hand van and a few thousand in savings, with his partner doing the books, and revisits the house once it earns.
S3.feel: A bit uneasy but mostly fired up.
S3.quote: Buy early and train us, or buy late and pay more.
S3.fieldNote: Gareth sees five years as his ideal window to build a business, and his plan has clear steps and numbers. He accepts the business won't last forever but values a few good years. He expects his boss to become a customer rather than an obstacle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd say there's no excuse for anyone to be caught out. I'd say farms should plan how they'll run, and governments should make sure the countryside doesn't empty out. Probably I'd be a bit of a bore about it at family dinners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be relaxed. Ten years means I can build the business slowly, and Jess can shift her work without a crisis. I'd be thirty-seven when it arrives, with hopefully a house and maybe a kid, and a good few years of being the person farms call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the technician course this year, build the call-out work slowly, and keep my job at Hallam for a few years longer than in the faster version. We'd go ahead with the house in about two years and try for a baby too, because we wouldn't want to put life on hold for a decade. I'd also put a small amount into robot company shares each year, like a hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a timetable, not a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the countryside emptying out. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If farms need three people instead of ten, the young families leave, the school shuts, and the pub goes. Eastford's primary school already has half the kids it had when I was there. That's the bit I'd want government to think about, not just the jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the slow version that does bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd get comfortable. With ten years, it's easy to think I'll always be the clever one with the robots, and then one day the robots don't need clever. I'd want Jess to remind me of that.

S4.say: I'd say with ten years nobody should be caught out, farms should plan how they'll run, and governments should stop the countryside emptying out. I'd be a bit of a bore about it at family dinners.
S4.think: I'd be relaxed, because ten years lets me build a business slowly and lets my partner shift her work without a crisis. At thirty-seven I'd hopefully have a house, maybe a child, and years of being the person farms call.
S4.do: Takes the technician course this year, builds call-out work slowly and stays at Hallam Farm longer. Goes ahead with the house in about two years and tries for a baby, and puts about a hundred a month into robot company shares.
S4.feel: Calm, like a timetable rather than a threat.
S4.quote: It's easy to think I'll always be the clever one with the robots, and then one day the robots don't need clever.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Gareth relaxes and lets family plans go ahead, which contrasts sharply with the two-year version. His bigger concern shifts to rural communities shrinking, illustrated by his old school's falling numbers. He is aware of his own risk of complacency.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it's the only one where Jess and I could both lose our income at once, and we'd have to put the family on hold. What would help is some kind of income support for a couple of years, and help for small rural businesses like the one I'd start, cheap loans maybe. Simple rules on who's responsible when a robot gets it wrong on a farm would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what the animals think, if that's not daft. Our cows took about two weeks to learn the robot milkers, and now they queue up on their own. They adapted faster than half the people in the village. I find that funny and a bit humbling.

headlineQuote: Our cows took about two weeks to learn the robot milkers, and now they queue up on their own. They adapted faster than half the people in the village.
portrait: Gareth Larsen is 27 and runs the robot milkers and much of the field work at Hallam Farm, a big dairy and arable farm, living in a rented terrace with his partner Jess, an accountant. He uses AI every day and is the person neighbours call when their tractor won't connect. Plateau and steady change leave him calm, even keen, though he worries that Jess's office job is more exposed than his. In the two-year AGI picture he'd chase short-term fitting work, buy a few robot company shares and put plans for children on hold. With five or ten years he sees a chance to build his own robot service business, while warning himself not to get complacent.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because he and Jess could both lose their income at once and would have to put their family plans on hold.
whatWouldHelp: Income support for a couple of years, cheap loans for small rural businesses, and clear rules on who is responsible when a farm robot gets something wrong.
